items.title: The chain rule explains why a car's acceleration depends on both gear and rpm
items.claim: A car's speed (v) depends on engine rpm (omega) through the gear ratio. Engine rpm depends on time as the driver presses the throttle. The chain rule says dv/dt = (dv/d(omega)) * (d(omega)/dt). Acceleration is the product of two derivatives.
items.prompt: What's the chain rule's geometric meaning?

options.text: When y depends on u and u depends on t, a small change in t produces a small change in u (scaled by du/dt) which produces a small change in y (scaled by dy/du); chaining the scalings gives dy/dt = (dy/du)(du/dt)
It is wrong for vector quantities

items.reveal_title: The chain rule as composition of rates
items.reveal:
If y = f(u) and u = g(t), then y = f(g(t)). The chain rule: dy/dt = f'(g(t)) * g'(t) = (dy/du) * (du/dt).

Geometric intuition: a small Delta t produces a small Delta u (approximately (du/dt) * Delta t), which produces a small Delta y (approximately (dy/du) * Delta u). Combining: Delta y ≈ (dy/du)(du/dt) Delta t. Take the limit and you get the chain rule.

Physics examples:
- A particle's position depends on time. Its velocity depends on its position (e.g., in a velocity field). Acceleration = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx. This is the Eulerian-Lagrangian connection in fluid mechanics.
- Optics: refractive index varies with position. The ray equation involves chain rules through the index.
- Thermodynamics: pressure depends on temperature and volume. Derivatives form a web of chain rules — Maxwell relations.

The chain rule is the BACKBONE of backpropagation in neural networks: gradients of a loss with respect to weights are computed via chain rules through layers of the network. Training deep neural networks is essentially repeated chain rule applications across millions of parameters.

When u or g has multiple components (vector-valued), the chain rule becomes the JACOBIAN rule — products of matrices of partial derivatives.
items.why: The chain rule looks like a notational identity. It's the fundamental principle of compositional change — appearing in physics, optimisation, neural networks, and any setting where one variable depends on another through an intermediate.

items.title: Integration by parts is the product rule played backwards
items.claim: The product rule: d(uv)/dx = u'v + uv'. Rearrange: uv' = d(uv)/dx - u'v. Integrate: integral of uv' dx = uv - integral of u'v dx. The formula isn't a separate tool — it's the product rule, integrated.

options.text: Choose u as the type higher in 'ILATE' priority: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential. These tend to become simpler when differentiated; choosing them as u makes u'v easier to integrate than the original

items.reveal_title: Integration by parts and clever choices
items.reveal:
Integration by parts: integral of u dv = uv - integral of v du.

The formula always works mathematically, but the resulting integral can be HARDER than the original if you choose u and dv poorly. The ILATE heuristic helps:
- I: Inverse trig (arctan, arcsin)
- L: Logarithmic (ln x)
- A: Algebraic (polynomials)
- T: Trigonometric (sin, cos)
- E: Exponential (e^x)

Choose u as the FIRST function appearing in this list. Choose dv as the LAST.

Why: logarithmic and inverse trig functions become algebraic when differentiated; polynomials become lower-degree polynomials. Exponentials and most trig functions stay similar under differentiation, so we'd rather integrate them.

Classical applications:
- integral of x e^x dx: u = x, dv = e^x dx. Result: x e^x - e^x + C.
- integral of x sin x dx: u = x, dv = sin x dx. Result: -x cos x + sin x + C.
- integral of ln x dx: u = ln x, dv = dx. Result: x ln x - x + C.
- integral of x^2 e^x dx: apply twice.

Tabular integration (D-I tabular method) systematises repeated applications.

The Frullani integral, Bessel functions, and many special-function identities come from clever integration by parts. It's not just a textbook drill; it's the algebraic shadow of one of the deepest theorems in calculus (the fundamental theorem applied to product structures).
items.why: Integration by parts is taught as a mechanical technique. It's the product rule running backwards — and the ILATE heuristic is empirical wisdom about which functions are easier to differentiate than integrate.

items.title: Your average speed never equals your speed at most moments
items.claim: Drive 60 miles in one hour at varying speeds — slowing for lights, accelerating onto highways. Average speed is 60 mph. But that doesn't mean you were doing 60 mph for most of the time. You may have spent more time at 30 mph than at 90 mph.
items.prompt: What's the difference between average and instantaneous?

options.text: Average and instantaneous are equal at the midpoint

Average speed = total distance / total time. Instantaneous speed = the limit of average speed over a vanishing interval — the derivative dx/dt. The mean value theorem guarantees at SOME instant the instantaneous speed equals the average, but not at most or all instants

items.reveal:
Mean Value Theorem (MVT): if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then there exists c in (a, b) such that f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a).

In driving terms: at SOME moment during your journey, your instantaneous speed was exactly equal to your average speed. (Not all moments — at least one.) This is the rigorous version of what intuition gets right.

Applications:
- Speed cameras using 'average speed enforcement': measure entry and exit times over a stretch; if average exceeds limit, you must have exceeded the limit at SOME moment (MVT). This is legally watertight.
- Optimisation: locating extrema where f'(c) = 0.
- L'Hopital's rule and Taylor's theorem are MVT consequences.

The full Taylor expansion exploits this: f(b) = f(a) + f'(a)(b-a) + (1/2)f''(a)(b-a)^2 + ... Each term corrects the linear approximation with higher-order behaviour. The remainder terms involve derivatives at intermediate points (Lagrange remainder).

Derivative as instantaneous rate: dx/dt at t = t_0 is the limit as h approaches 0 of (x(t_0 + h) - x(t_0)) / h. Defined when this limit exists. It tells you the rate of change exactly at time t_0 — not over any finite interval.

Velocity (vector) vs speed (scalar magnitude). At a U-turn, average velocity over the round trip is zero (you end up back where you started), but average speed is non-zero. Distinguishing them is key in kinematics.
items.why: Average rates feel like reliable summaries of what happened. The mean value theorem guarantees only ONE instant matches the average; for most of a journey, instantaneous speed differs. Speed limits use both.
